tldr: We propose "Q-Planning," where a robot continuously and autonomously improves its performance by leaving a massive imitation learning policy completely untouched and training only a small, sidecar Q-function on failure data.
hero_caption: Overview of Q-Planning. On the left, action candidates are generated from a frozen BC policy, and a Q-weighted average is executed. On the right, both successful and failed deployment rollouts are accumulated in a buffer, fine-tuning only the Q-function to loop into the next inference cycle.
overview:
In recent robot manipulation, large Behaviour Cloning (BC) models trained on extensive human teleoperation data have achieved remarkable results. However, BC models face a fundamental limitation: they cannot learn from failures. If a robot fails during autonomous execution, it cannot turn that failure into future improvement without additional human demonstrations. Reinforcement learning fine-tuning has been actively explored, but directly updating multi-billion-parameter Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models incurs heavy computational costs and constantly risks catastrophic forgetting of their underlying dexterous behaviors.

To address this, the authors reached a simple insight: separate the data handled by the actor (action generation) and the critic (value evaluation) asymmetrically. While a BC policy can only learn to imitate successes, a Q-function that evaluates value can learn off-policy from past data containing both successes and failures. Exploiting this property, they built "Q-Planning," a framework that keeps the massive BC policy completely frozen and updates only a lightweight, roughly 1-billion-parameter Q-function placed alongside it.

In experiments across simulation benchmarks (LIBERO and bimanual RoboTwin), simply running the self-improvement loop substantially lifted success rates in all environments. Furthermore, on challenging contact-rich bimanual real-robot tasks, they demonstrated dramatic improvements from 40% to 90% and 25% to 80% without additional human intervention, purely by absorbing the robot's own failure experiences.
contributions: Proposed "Q-Planning," a self-improvement framework combining a fully frozen, massive BC policy with an off-policy Q-function capable of absorbing failure data.
Developed a single-step Q-weighted average over multiple candidates drawn from the BC policy at inference time, achieving fast planning that fits within real-time control constraints.
Showed that fine-tuning only the Q-function rather than full model weights stably drives improvement from failures without degrading the original BC policy's capabilities.
Successfully demonstrated dramatic, autonomous success-rate improvements on contact-rich real-world bimanual robot tasks without any additional human demonstrations.

sections.heading: Beyond imitation: A new concept for self-improvement with a frozen BC model
sections.summary: Large-scale Behaviour Cloning (BC) makes robots dexterous, but it cannot transcend human demonstrations or learn from failures. This work proposes a self-improvement loop that safely and efficiently absorbs failure data by freezing the BC policy and updating only a small Q-function.
sections.details:
Large Behaviour Cloning (BC) models such as RT-2 and Diffusion Policy have shown remarkable results, including zero-shot generalization. However, because BC is a method that imitates successful actions present in the training data, failing during autonomous operation provides no route to improvement unless a human collects additional demonstrations. With model scales reaching billions of parameters, this demonstration ceiling has become the primary bottleneck.

The standard alternative is reinforcement learning fine-tuning. Yet directly updating a massive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model is computationally demanding and prone to instability. In the worst case, it destroys the capable behavioral foundation the BC policy originally possessed.

The breakthrough here lies in separating the action-generating actor from the value-estimating critic and training them on different data distributions. A BC policy cannot be taught to imitate failures, so it only learns from successful data. A Q-function that estimates action values carries no such constraint. From any trajectory, successful or failed, it can learn whether an action was good or bad off-policy (the property of learning from data collected under any policy). By exploiting this asymmetry, keeping the massive BC policy frozen and letting only a lightweight sidecar Q-function absorb failure experiences yields safe, efficient self-improvement.

sections.heading: How does it differ from existing RL and planning?
sections.summary: Existing VLA update methods risk degrading the entire model, and value-guided methods have not handled online self-improvement. Q-Planning is the only method that simultaneously achieves a frozen BC policy, no auxiliary actor, and self-improvement from failures.
sections.details:
Research into value functions and planning for robot control has a long history, but in VLA models with continuous, high-dimensional action spaces, planning over random exploratory candidates is computationally intractable. Furthermore, recent value-guided methods (which guide policies using pretrained value functions) only leverage offline-learned values and lack an online loop for autonomous self-improvement.

Meanwhile, actively fine-tuning large policies via online reinforcement learning consumes vast compute by updating all parameters across the massive network, risking degradation of the original imitation performance. Other methods like IBRL train a separate RL actor from scratch alongside a frozen imitation model, but this requires relearning the dexterous behaviors the BC policy already mastered from scratch, which fails to scale.

Q-Planning stands out by satisfying all of the following:
- Keeping the base large BC policy weights completely frozen
- Introducing no auxiliary actor trained from scratch
- Stably self-improving from failed rollouts

This makes it possible to preserve 100% of the foundation model's strengths while rapidly absorbing on-site deployment experience.

sections.heading: How Q-Planning works: Q-chunking and single-step weighted averaging
sections.summary: The approach consists of three parts: a Q-function over action chunks, inference via Q-weighted averaging of BC candidates, and a self-improvement loop updating only the Q-function. Leveraging BC multi-modality, it selects high-quality actions within real-time limits without iterative search.
sections.details:
The overall architecture and algorithm of Q-Planning consist of the following three components:

### 3.1 & 3.2 Off-policy Q-function over action chunks
Robot manipulation typically features sparse rewards provided only upon task completion, causing estimation errors to compound and break learning under standard scalar Q-learning. The method adopts two key mechanisms:
1. **Q-chunking**: Rather than evaluating single-step actions, a sequence of continuous actions of length $H$ (an action chunk) is treated as a single macro-action. This reduces the number of bootstrapping steps (computing current value from next-state value) by a factor of $1/H$, preventing error explosion.
2. **HL-Gauss classification representation**: Instead of regressing scalar values directly, targets are projected onto fixed bins as Gaussian distributions and trained with cross-entropy loss. This stabilizes value learning even under extremely sparse reward settings.

The Q-function network comprises roughly 1 billion parameters, consisting of a vision encoder (DinoV2), a text encoder (T5), and a transformer decoder that consumes candidate chunks. Because its parameters are entirely decoupled from the BC policy, updating the Q-function structurally cannot corrupt the BC model.

### 3.3 Real-time action selection via Q-weighting
At inference time, $N$ candidate action chunks are sampled from the BC policy (a Flow Matching model) given current observations. Because Flow Matching generation is multimodal (capable of presenting distinct ways of solving the task), it yields diverse, meaningful candidates, unlike Gaussian noise exploring around a single mean.

Each candidate is scored by the Q-function, and a weighted average $\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{t:t+H} = \sum_{n} \frac{\exp(Q(a^{(n)})/\lambda)}{\sum_j \exp(Q(a^{(j)})/\lambda)} \mathbf{a}^{(n)}$ using softmax temperature $\lambda$ is computed and executed. Image and text encoding run only once per step, and the decoder evaluates all candidates in parallel. The entire process takes only around 400ms, well within the robot control period (the 960ms replanning budget).

### 3.4 Self-improvement loop
The planner is deployed in the environment to execute tasks, saving both successful and failed trajectories to a replay buffer. Minibatches are sampled from the buffer to fine-tune only the Q-function via gradient descent. Failed trajectories naturally pull Q-learning targets down to zero as zero-reward terminal data, evolving the value function to avoid failures without bespoke adjustments.

captions.F1: The cycle from offline imitation learning to online self-improvement. The BC policy remains frozen from start to finish, and all rollout feedback—both successes and failures—is channeled exclusively into the Q-function.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Learning from failure to conquer hard benchmarks and real-robot tasks
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted in simulation (LIBERO, RoboTwin) and on a bimanual real robot. In simulation, 10 iterations improved scores across all environments. On the real robot, success rates jumped from 40% to 90% and 25% to 80% without additional human intervention.
sections.details:
Using FastWAM as the base BC model, the experiments evaluated four primary questions:

### Q1: What action candidates should be used for planning?
When compared to conventional MPPI (iterative sampling with Gaussian noise), standard MPPI produced unnatural trajectories that drifted out of the BC distribution due to Gaussian perturbations, leading to Q-function overestimation and worse performance than the standalone FastWAM baseline. A single-step Q-weighted average over candidates sampled directly from BC achieved performance matching or exceeding temporally smoothed MPPI, while running 1.7x to 3.2x faster.

### Q2 & Q3: How far does online self-improvement scale?
Across simulation suites (LIBERO-10 and 47 tasks in RoboTwin), 10 self-improvement iterations were performed:
- **LIBERO-10**: Success rate improved from $93\% \to 99\%$
- **RoboTwin**: Success rate improved from $83.8\% \to 91.4\%$
- On near-ceiling suites (LIBERO-Object, Goal), task completion steps were shortened, refining behaviors.

Compared to alternative methods, Filtered SFT (fine-tuning only on successful rollouts) plateaued at 93.5%, underscoring the benefit of Q-Planning's failure-driven learning. While IBRL collapsed mid-training and DSRL showed volatile fluctuations, only Q-Planning sustained stable score increases.

### Q4: Can a real robot learn autonomously from failures?
Using two 6-DoF arms, the authors tackled two contact-rich, precision-demanding tasks (stacking cups and inserting a card into a wallet). Without any additional human teleoperation—only resetting between episodes and assigning success labels—five iterations of the loop yielded:
- **Stacking cups**: Success rate $40\% \to 90\%$
- **Inserting card into wallet**: Success rate $25\% \to 80\%$

In contrast, SFT baselines fine-tuned purely on successes stalled at 55% and 30%, respectively, proving that incorporating failure rollouts into the Q-function directly drives dramatic real-world progress.

captions.F4: Two contact-rich tasks on a real bimanual robot (left: cup stacking, right: card insertion into a wallet). Even on tasks requiring delicate alignment, learning from its own failures lifted success rates substantially.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A realistic path to self-improvement in the era of massive policies
sections.summary: Q-Planning is a smart framework exploiting the asymmetry that BC can only imitate success, whereas Q-functions can learn from failures. It offers a highly practical approach for robotics AI as models continue to scale.
sections.details:
The most important takeaway from this work is that robots can improve dramatically simply by cultivating a discerning evaluator (Q-function), without ever modifying the policy itself.

As VLA models exceed 10 billion parameters, end-to-end RL fine-tuning across entire networks becomes exceptionally difficult in terms of compute and operation. However, by updating only the roughly 1-billion-parameter Q-function with deployment rollouts as in Q-Planning, training cost depends strictly on critic size, scaling cleanly into the future.

Furthermore, this framework is not limited strictly to BC policies; it holds potential for any generator capable of outputting diverse, plausible action candidates, including offline RL policies and world models.

takeaways: Leaving the massive imitation learning (BC) policy frozen prevents catastrophic forgetting while safely driving performance gains.
Because the Q-function learns off-policy from failure data (reward 0), it neatly compensates for BC's inherent inability to learn from anything but success.
A single-step Q-weighted average over diverse Flow Matching candidates enables high-quality planning within real-time budgets (400ms) without iterative search methods like MPPI.
Incorporating failure learning on real-world robots shatters the performance ceiling that stalls methods like SFT, which only retrain on successful rollouts.
limitations: In completely unseen tasks where the base BC policy cannot produce any successful candidate actions, self-improvement has no exploratory foothold and cannot proceed.
Scaling the candidate count $N$ into the hundreds increases Q-function decoder computation linearly, potentially exceeding real-time control constraints.
Executing the self-improvement loop requires an external signal (such as a success detector) to evaluate success or failure at the end of each episode.
